south dakota.repose_note: South Dakota has no statute of repose for product liability; its former six-year repose period was repealed in 1985.
south dakota.sol_note: A product-liability action must be filed within three years of when the injury occurred or became known or should have become known.
south dakota.state_note: A store or distributor that did not make the product is immune from strict liability unless it also made the product or knew or should have known of the defect.
south dakota.strict_note: South Dakota allows strict-liability claims against a manufacturer for a defective product, but non-manufacturing sellers are immune unless they made the product or knew or should have known of the defect.

tennessee.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands
tennessee.repose_note: A claim must be brought within ten years from the date the product was first purchased for use or consumption, or within one year after the product's anticipated life expires, whichever is shorter, and in any event within six years of the injury.
tennessee.sol_note: A personal-injury product claim must be filed within one year after the cause of action accrues, generally the date of injury.
tennessee.state_note: Tennessee caps noneconomic damages at $750,000 in most personal-injury cases.
tennessee.strict_note: Tennessee's Products Liability Act covers claims based on strict liability as well as negligence and warranty.

texas.repose_note: A product-liability claim generally must be filed within 15 years after the date the defendant sold the product.
texas.sol_note: A personal-injury suit must be filed within two years after the cause of action accrues, with a discovery rule for harm that is not immediately apparent.
texas.state_note: A seller that did not manufacture the product is generally not liable unless one of the exceptions in Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code section 82.003 applies, such as the manufacturer being insolvent or outside the court's jurisdiction.
texas.statute_cite: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code ch. 82
texas.strict_note: Texas adopted strict liability under Restatement (Second) of Torts section 402A, so a claimant need not prove the manufacturer was negligent.

utah.repose_note: Utah's Product Liability Act sets a two-year limitations period but contains no statute of repose for product claims.
utah.sol_note: A claim must be filed within two years from when the claimant discovered, or should have discovered, both the harm and its cause.
utah.state_note: Utah voids contract clauses that make a buyer indemnify or defend a product manufacturer.
utah.strict_note: Utah adopted strict liability under Restatement (Second) section 402A in 1979, so a defective, unreasonably dangerous product can support liability without proof of negligence.

vermont.repose_note: Vermont has no general statute of repose for product liability.
vermont.sol_note: A product-liability claim must be filed within three years, with the clock starting when the injury is discovered.
vermont.state_note: Vermont has a separate 20-year outer limit only for injuries from ionizing radiation or other noxious agents with prolonged latent development, not for ordinary product claims.
vermont.strict_note: Vermont adopted strict liability for defective products in Zaleskie v. Joyce (1975).

virginia.repose_note: Virginia has no general statute of repose for product liability; the five-year limit in Va. Code section 8.01-250 applies only to defective improvements to real property.
virginia.sol_note: A claim must be filed within two years from the date the injury is sustained, with no general discovery rule except for asbestos, breast-implant, and implanted-device cases.
virginia.state_note: Virginia follows pure contributory negligence, so being even 1% at fault can bar recovery.
virginia.strict_note: Virginia is one of the few states that never adopted strict liability in tort for products, so an injured person must prove negligence or breach of warranty.

washington.repose_note: Washington has no hard statute of repose, but harm occurring more than 12 years after delivery is presumed to be past the product's useful safe life, a presumption the claimant may rebut.
washington.sol_note: A claim must be filed within three years from when the claimant discovered, or should have discovered, the harm and its cause.
washington.state_note: Washington uses pure comparative fault, so partial fault reduces recovery but does not bar it.
washington.strict_note: Washington imposes strict liability for a product that is not reasonably safe in construction or does not conform to warranty, while design and warning claims require proof of the manufacturer's negligence.

west virginia.repose_note: West Virginia has no statute of repose for product liability.
west virginia.sol_note: A claim must be filed within two years, and the clock starts when the plaintiff knows or should know of the injury, the maker's identity, and the product's causal role.
west virginia.state_note: An innocent seller is generally shielded from product-liability claims unless it knew of the defect, controlled the design, or altered the product.
west virginia.strict_note: West Virginia adopted strict liability for defective products in Morningstar v. Black & Decker (1979).

wisconsin.repose_note: A defendant is not liable under Wisconsin's strict-liability statute if the product was manufactured 15 years or more before the claim accrued, unless the manufacturer promised a longer life.
wisconsin.sol_note: A personal-injury product claim must be filed within three years after the cause of action accrues.
wisconsin.state_note: Wisconsin's 15-year limit does not apply to claims for damages caused by a latent disease.
wisconsin.strict_note: Wisconsin's statute expressly provides for strict-liability claims against a manufacturer whose defective product caused harm.

wyoming.repose_note: Wyoming has no general statute of repose for product liability; its separate 10-year limit covers only claims tied to improvements to real property.
wyoming.sol_note: A product-liability claim must be filed within four years, with a discovery rule for injuries that are not immediately apparent.
wyoming.state_note: Wyoming's constitution bars caps on damages, so there is no statutory ceiling on a product-liability award.
wyoming.strict_note: Wyoming adopted strict liability for defective products in Ogle v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1986).
